name: Classic Highly Available Web Application
description: A traditional, highly available three-tier web application architecture hosted on AWS using managed services. It spans multiple Availability Zones to ensure high availability and uses Application Load Balancers for traffic distribution.
retrieval_text: A classic highly available web application architecture spanning multiple Availability Zones. It routes traffic via Amazon Route 53 and accelerates content delivery with Amazon CloudFront. AWS WAF protects against web exploits, while AWS Certificate Manager simplifies SSL/TLS management. An internet-facing Application Load Balancer distributes incoming traffic to a web tier of Amazon EC2 instances within an Auto Scaling group. These web servers route requests to an internal Application Load Balancer, which distributes traffic to application tier EC2 instances. Amazon RDS provides a highly available primary and standby database in a Database subnet group. Amazon ElastiCache handles caching for read-heavy access patterns, and Amazon EFS provides shared storage for servers. Amazon S3 is used for static storage and backups. NAT Gateways allow instances in private subnets to access the internet. This pattern is ideal for traditional web applications, monoliths, and enterprise workloads needing high availability and relational databases.
use_cases: Applications requiring file sharing across instances

name: Serverless Single-Page Application (SPA)
description: A serverless web application architecture using Amazon S3 for static frontend hosting, CloudFront for content delivery, and API Gateway with AWS Lambda for the backend logic.
retrieval_text: A serverless single-page application (SPA) architecture suitable for modern web applications. Static frontend content (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) is hosted in an Amazon S3 bucket and distributed globally by Amazon CloudFront, utilizing AWS Certificate Manager for custom SSL/TLS certificates. The frontend client issues HTTPS requests via a custom domain managed by Amazon Route 53 to Amazon API Gateway. API Gateway is secured using a Lambda Authorizer, which verifies tokens obtained by the client from a third-party Identity Provider (e.g., Facebook, Google). API Gateway invokes AWS Lambda functions for backend microservices (/tickets, /shows, /info). These functions assume specific IAM roles to securely interact with the data tier. Amazon DynamoDB serves as the primary NoSQL data store, while Amazon ElastiCache is used to improve performance by caching database queries. Amazon S3 is also used by backend services to store and retrieve application files. This pattern is ideal for scalable web applications, serverless backends, variable traffic, and low-operations workloads.

name: Serverless Mobile Backend
description: A serverless multi-tier architecture for mobile backends using API Gateway, Lambda, Cognito, and a mix of NoSQL and relational databases.
retrieval_text: A serverless multi-tier architecture tailored for mobile application backends. The mobile client authenticates users via an Amazon Cognito User Pool (with optional third-party identity provider federation) and receives tokens. The client sends HTTPS requests including these tokens to Amazon API Gateway. API Gateway verifies the tokens with Cognito and forwards the request to specific AWS Lambda functions (/tickets, /shows, /info) acting as microservices. Lambda functions are assigned specific IAM execution roles for least-privilege data access. The architecture demonstrates mixed data tier strategies: some Lambda functions read/write to Amazon DynamoDB for NoSQL persistence, while others connect to a private subnet within an Amazon VPC using an Elastic Network Interface (ENI) to interact with an Amazon RDS relational database. Database credentials for RDS are securely retrieved at runtime using AWS Secrets Manager. This pattern is ideal for serverless mobile backends, handling variable mobile traffic, and integrating both NoSQL and relational data securely.
use_cases: Applications requiring both NoSQL and relational databases

name: Serverless Microservices with AWS Fargate
description: A serverless microservices architecture utilizing AWS Fargate for containerized compute and Amazon Aurora Serverless for on-demand relational databases.
retrieval_text: A serverless microservice architecture utilizing containers to remove the need for underlying infrastructure management. The user interface consists of static assets served by Amazon S3 and delivered globally via Amazon CloudFront. API requests are routed through Amazon API Gateway to an Application Load Balancer. The Application Load Balancer distributes traffic to containerized microservices running on AWS Fargate, an engine for Amazon ECS or EKS that requires no server provisioning. The data tier utilizes Amazon Aurora (often Serverless) and Amazon DynamoDB, providing automatic scaling capacity based on the application's requirements. This pattern is ideal for containerized microservices, API-driven architectures, and workloads where teams want to use Docker containers without managing EC2 instances.
use_cases: Modernizing legacy web applications to containers
Teams with Docker expertise seeking serverless ops

name: Event Sourcing Pattern on AWS
description: An event sourcing architecture that centralizes state changes as a sequence of events using Kinesis Data Streams and event processing microservices.
retrieval_text: An event sourcing architecture that captures all application changes as a timeline of events. An API Gateway exposes endpoints that invoke an AWS Lambda function (Microservice 1), which publishes events to a central Event Store powered by Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. For durable persistent event storage, Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose continuously archives the event stream to Amazon S3, which can be further loaded into Amazon Redshift for complex querying. Downstream microservices (Microservice 2 and 3) act as read and filter services or event processors by directly consuming the Kinesis Data Stream via AWS Lambda functions, subsequently updating materialized views in Amazon DynamoDB. This pattern allows different parts of an application to react to the same events, helps debug and audit system state, and pairs well with Command Query Responsibility Segregation (CQRS) patterns. Suitable for highly decoupled event-driven systems, auditing, and asynchronous processing.

strengths: Complete audit trail of state changes

constraints: Consumers must be designed to handle potential duplicate messages

name: Serverless SaaS Architecture
description: A multi-tenant serverless SaaS architecture using API Gateway, Lambda, and Cognito, isolating tenant data while sharing compute infrastructure.
retrieval_text: A Serverless SaaS (Software as a Service) architecture designed to maximize cost and operational efficiency in a multi-tenant environment. The web application, hosted via Amazon S3 and CloudFront, uses Amazon Cognito as the SaaS identity provider. Authentication yields a JSON Web Token (JWT) encapsulating the tenant context. Amazon API Gateway orchestrates requests, validates the JWT via a Lambda authorizer, maps tenant requests to microservices, and manages SLAs using usage plans. The architecture relies entirely on AWS Lambda for the application's multi-tenant microservices, utilizing the incoming JWT to acquire and apply tenant context dynamically at runtime for isolation (e.g., scoping DynamoDB or Aurora access). A dedicated block of 'Shared Services' (Registration, User Manager, Tenant Manager, Billing, System Admin) implemented in Lambda provides horizontal concepts spanning all tenants. This pattern is ideal for scalable, multi-tenant SaaS, low-operations workloads, and aligning infrastructure consumption directly with tenant activity.

name: Amazon EKS SaaS Architecture
description: A multi-tenant SaaS architecture running on Amazon EKS, using Kubernetes namespaces and pod security policies for tenant isolation.
retrieval_text: A container-based SaaS architecture using Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) to deploy multi-tenant microservices. This model uses shared Kubernetes clusters spanning multiple Availability Zones. An NGINX Ingress Controller directs incoming tenant traffic via Amazon Route 53 to appropriate services. The cluster contains a set of Shared Services (Registration, Tenant Management via DynamoDB, User Management via Cognito) provisioned to handle horizontal SaaS concepts. Crucially, tenant isolation is achieved by provisioning separate Kubernetes namespaces for each tenant environment (e.g., Tenant 1 namespace, Tenant 2 namespace). Inside these namespaces, tenant-specific application microservices (Order, Product) are deployed. Native Kubernetes pod security policies restrict cross-namespace network access, acting as coarse-grained isolation. Furthermore, AWS IAM policies restrict resource access (e.g., table-per-tenant or item-level row isolation in DynamoDB) ensuring stringent data segregation. This pattern is suitable for SaaS providers wanting container portability, Kubernetes tooling, and strong logical isolation boundaries for multi-tenancy.
use_cases: SaaS requiring isolated compute environments per tenant

name: Full Stack (Silo) Isolation SaaS
description: A SaaS deployment pattern where every tenant receives a completely dedicated, isolated AWS infrastructure stack (VPC per tenant) managed centrally.
retrieval_text: A full stack isolation (silo) SaaS architecture designed for environments with strict compliance, regulatory, or noisy neighbor requirements. Unlike pooled models, each tenant receives a completely dedicated infrastructure stack within their own Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) spanning multiple Availability Zones with Auto Scaling groups. Amazon Route 53 is used to route incoming traffic based on tenant-assigned subdomains (e.g., tenant1.abc.com) to the corresponding tenant VPC. Crucially, despite infrastructure isolation, this is a true SaaS model because a separate centralized 'SaaS Management and Operations' plane governs all tenants. This management plane (using API Gateway, Lambda, Cognito) handles unified onboarding, billing, metrics, and identity, interacting cross-VPC (via PrivateLink, Peering, or EventBridge) to configure and deploy the identical software version to all tenant VPCs. Ideal for high-compliance domains, legacy application migrations to SaaS, or premium tenant tiers demanding dedicated resources.
use_cases: Premium SaaS tiers requiring dedicated resources

name: AWS Security Reference Architecture (SRA) - Core Multi-Account
description: A foundational multi-account security architecture leveraging AWS Organizations, separating concerns into dedicated accounts like Security Tooling, Log Archive, Network, and Application workloads.
retrieval_text: The foundational AWS Security Reference Architecture (SRA) representing a robust multi-account strategy using AWS Organizations. It structures an environment into functional Organizational Units (OUs). The Org Management account hosts AWS Control Tower, IAM Identity Center, and organizational policies (SCPs). A dedicated 'Security OU' contains the Security Tooling account (acting as delegated administrator for AWS Security Hub, GuardDuty, Macie, Inspector, Config, etc.) and the Log Archive account (centralizing CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and Security Lake). An 'Infrastructure OU' isolates the Network account (managing Transit Gateway, AWS Network Firewall, Route 53 DNS Firewall, Inbound/Outbound VPCs) and a Shared Services account (hosting AWS Managed Microsoft AD). Workloads are isolated in an 'Application account' within a Workloads OU. This pattern establishes strong separation of duties, defense-in-depth, centralized security monitoring, and distributed enforcement, making it the mandatory baseline for enterprise-grade AWS deployments.

name: Serverless Data Lake Framework
description: An event-driven serverless data lake architecture for orchestrating data ingestion, transformation, and analytics using Step Functions, Glue, and Athena.
retrieval_text: An automated Serverless Data Lake Framework architecture for ingesting, transforming, and querying data. A data administrator uploads raw JSON files to an Amazon S3 Raw bucket, triggering an Amazon EventBridge rule that sends a message to Amazon SQS. SQS invokes an AWS Lambda function that initiates an AWS Step Functions workflow. Within the workflow, Lambda reads the raw data, transforms it, and writes it to an S3 Stage bucket, while logging status in Amazon DynamoDB. The stage bucket creation triggers another EventBridge/SQS/Lambda flow, managed by an EventBridge scheduler, which starts a second Step Functions workflow. This workflow uses AWS Glue ETL to convert the JSON files to Parquet format, storing them in an S3 Analytics bucket. An AWS Glue Crawler then builds the schema in the AWS Glue Data Catalog. Finally, business analysts use Amazon Athena to execute serverless SQL queries against the optimized Parquet data. This pattern is ideal for automated, serverless data pipelines, unstructured data ingestion, and scalable analytics/lakehouse architectures.
use_cases: Transforming raw data into query-optimized formats (Parquet)

name: Multi-Source Analytics Lakehouse with AI-Powered Insights
description: A comprehensive Lakehouse architecture integrating streaming, operational databases, and third-party data using Zero-ETL, governed by Lake Formation and analyzed using Amazon Bedrock and Athena.
retrieval_text: An advanced Multi-Source Analytics Lakehouse architecture combining data lakes and warehouses. In the Producer Account, streaming inventory data is ingested via Amazon Kinesis Data Streams and Amazon Data Firehose into Amazon S3 Tables. Operational data from Amazon Aurora and SAP is ingested into Amazon Redshift Serverless and Amazon S3 (Apache Iceberg format) via AWS Glue using Zero-ETL integrations. Data is cataloged in Lakehouse for Amazon SageMaker as a federated catalog managed by AWS Lake Formation. A Central Governance Account controls access and governance using Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio. Consumer Accounts subscribe to the data, allowing Data Engineers to run Spark jobs on Amazon EC2 via an open Iceberg REST API, while Marketing Analysts use Amazon Athena and Amazon QuickSight to query and visualize the unified data. Sales Analysts leverage Generative AI by querying unified data using natural language through Amazon Bedrock foundation models and Knowledge Bases with Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG). Ideal for enterprise lakehouses, Zero-ETL pipelines, and AI-driven analytics.

name: Ecommerce Web Application Architecture
description: A comprehensive, highly scalable ecommerce architecture using AWS Fargate, API Gateway, EventBridge, and specialized services like Personalize and Fraud Detector.
retrieval_text: A highly scalable ecommerce web application architecture blending containerized microservices and event-driven patterns. Users access a headless, responsive Web Tier (React/Vue deployed on AWS Fargate) routed through Amazon Route 53, CloudFront, and an Application Load Balancer, secured by AWS WAF. Amazon Cognito provides authentication. The Web Tier invokes backend APIs via Amazon API Gateway, backed by stateless Ecommerce Microservices (App Tier) running on AWS Fargate and AWS Lambda. Amazon DynamoDB serves as the primary data store (with DynamoDB Accelerator/DAX), while Amazon ElastiCache caches microservice responses. Amazon EventBridge orchestrates asynchronous, event-driven workflows (e.g., user sign-ups or order processing). A suite of managed services enhances the platform: Amazon OpenSearch Service for product search, Amazon Personalize for AI-driven recommendations, Amazon Pinpoint for marketing, Amazon Location Service for delivery tracking, Amazon Fraud Detector for transaction security, and Amazon Lex for chatbots. Amazon SQS handles order messaging, while Amazon MSK manages high-throughput ETL data feeds (e.g., catalog/inventory). This pattern is robustly designed for global ecommerce scale.
use_cases: Retail applications requiring AI/ML integrations (recommendations, fraud)

name: Serverless In-Game Screenshot Processing Pipeline
description: A serverless event-driven pipeline for receiving, validating (profanity filtering), processing, and serving in-game screenshots to a community site.
retrieval_text: A serverless architecture designed to process in-game screenshots for gaming studios. A game client uploads a screenshot by invoking an Amazon API Gateway REST endpoint secured by Amazon Cognito. API Gateway triggers an 'Image Uploader/Processor' AWS Lambda function. This function pre-processes the image by sending it to Amazon Rekognition (using the DetectModerationLabels API) to filter out profanity or inappropriate content. The results can trigger notifications via Amazon SNS. The raw image is optionally stored in an Amazon S3 'raw' bucket. The Lambda function then resizes or watermarks the image, uploading the final version to an S3 'processed' bucket, and extracts metadata (player ID, timestamp) to store in Amazon DynamoDB along with the S3 object key. When a community site or game client requests the gallery, API Gateway triggers an 'Image Retrieval' Lambda function that queries DynamoDB for the image URLs, and the images are served globally via Amazon CloudFront from the processed S3 bucket. Ideal for automated content moderation, image processing pipelines, and user-generated content validation.
use_cases: Automated image resizing and watermarking platforms

name: Multi-Region API Gateway with CloudFront Architecture
description: An active-active multi-region API architecture leveraging Amazon CloudFront, Lambda@Edge for routing, API Gateway, and Amazon Aurora Global Database for data synchronization.
retrieval_text: A multi-region architecture designed to reduce latency for global end-users and increase application availability. A custom domain with an SSL certificate from AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) is attached to an Amazon CloudFront distribution, with Amazon Route 53 resolving the DNS. CloudFront provides global edge caching. To seamlessly authenticate and route requests, AWS Lambda@Edge executes routing logic at the edge locations, querying Route 53 to determine the AWS Region with the lowest latency to the client's location, normalizing authorization by abstracting regional endpoints. The request is forwarded to an Amazon API Gateway endpoint deployed in the selected Region (e.g., Region A or Region B). API Gateway invokes local AWS Lambda handler functions. To ensure data consistency across regions, the Lambda functions connect to an Amazon Aurora Global Database. Aurora automatically routes write requests to the primary node for transactions and replicates changes to secondary nodes across all deployed AWS Regions with sub-second latency. This pattern is suitable for global APIs, active-active multi-region deployments, low latency API architectures, and disaster recovery.
use_cases: Global API endpoints requiring low latency worldwide

name: Saga Execution Coordinator Pattern
description: A microservices orchestration pattern using AWS Step Functions to manage distributed transactions and compensating actions across multiple services.
retrieval_text: A Saga execution coordinator pattern designed to handle complex distributed transactions across microservices where a single shared database is not available. This architecture uses AWS Step Functions as a central workflow engine to coordinate a series of steps. The workflow starts by executing a 'CreateOrder' step, saving state to Amazon DynamoDB. It proceeds to a 'ProcessPayment' AWS Lambda function. If payment succeeds, it updates the customer account and sets the order as completed. If any step fails, the Saga pattern ensures data consistency by executing compensating actions. For example, if 'UpdateCustomerAccount' fails, the workflow branches to a 'SetOrderFailed' state in DynamoDB, triggers a 'RefundCustomer' Lambda function to reverse the payment, and sends an 'OrderFailed' notification via Amazon SNS. This orchestration ensures that either all operations complete successfully or all compensating transactions execute, maintaining overall system consistency. Ideal for e-commerce checkouts, complex order fulfillment, and orchestrating distributed state management.

constraints: Compensating transactions must be carefully designed to be idempotent

name: Message Bus (Publish-Subscribe) Pattern
description: An asynchronous messaging architecture using Amazon SNS and Amazon SQS to decouple microservices and distribute events to multiple consumers.
retrieval_text: A fundamental Message Bus (publish-subscribe) architecture pattern for loosely coupled asynchronous microservices communication. A Provider Microservice (e.g., hosted on Amazon EC2) publishes an important event to a Message Bus. The bus is implemented using an Amazon SNS topic. The SNS topic fans out the message to multiple destination Amazon SQS queues. Consumer Microservices (B and C) running on their respective compute environments (e.g., Amazon EC2) continuously poll their dedicated SQS queues to process the events at their own pace. This pattern decouples senders from receivers, provides a buffer for handling bursts of traffic (load leveling), and enables broadcasting events asynchronously. It is highly suitable for event-driven systems where the same message must be delivered to multiple downstream destinations reliably without blocking the publisher.
use_cases: Broadcasting state changes to multiple services
Decoupling heavy backend processing from fast frontend APIs
